--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.attracting_components()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Find the attracting components of a directed graph. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.attracting_components()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Find the attracting components of a directed graph. title: >- [Graph.attracting_components()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Find the attracting components of a directed graph. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find the attracting components of a directed graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L84712-L84827){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.attracting_components() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Attracting components](../assets/graphs/attracting-components.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A directed graph: A points to B and to D, and B and C point to each other. A random walk that leaves A never comes back: it ends up circling B and C or stuck at D. Those are the attracting components, D in the accent color and B, C in teal, listed on the card as {D} and {B, C}; A, in neither, is faded." width="100%"} An attracting component is a strongly connected component with no edges leaving it: once a walk enters, it can never leave. They are the "sinks" of the condensation. In a Markov chain they are the closed communicating classes, which hold all of the long-run probability; in a web or citation graph they are traps for random surfers; in a state machine they are terminal behaviors. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[set[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The attracting components as sets of node IDs. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is undirected. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Strongly connected components are found first; a component is attracting when no edge goes from it to another component, $O(V + E)$ in total. Matches NetworkX's `attracting_components`. ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~strongly_connected_components`) : Every strongly connected component. [](`~is_attracting_component`) : Check whether the whole graph is one. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A walk on this graph ends up either going around `B` and `C` or stuck at `D`. `A` can be left, and so it belongs to no attracting component: ::: {#6a84f39d .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "B"), ("A", "D")], directed=True ) label = graph.get_label_from_id [sorted(label(n) for n in c) for c in graph.attracting_components()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [['D'], ['B', 'C']] ``` ::: ::: A directed cycle is strongly connected with nowhere to go, so the whole graph is one attracting component: ::: {#cd6ef45a .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} ring = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_cycle_graph(4) len(ring.attracting_components()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 1 ``` ::: ::: ### Where the money ends up `payments()` is a month of payments between 18 accounts at a made-up bank, each directed from payer to payee. Every chain of payments ends at one of three businesses that pay no one, so money that reaches them stays there: the Landlord, the Cafe and the Grocer: ::: {#9ef28ece .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} payments = ec.payments() sinks = payments.attracting_components() label = payments.get_label_from_id [label(n) for c in sinks for n in c] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ['Landlord', 'Cafe', 'Grocer'] ``` ::: ::: ::: {#47a72d24 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} payments.plot( highlight=[n for c in sinks for n in c], label_by="label", seed=3 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ### The top of a food chain `food_web()` is a made-up woodland food web, with an edge from each food to each species that eats it. Energy flowing up the web ends at the three species that nothing eats, the Fox, the Hawk and the Marten, so each is an attracting component of its own: ::: {#2eda067a .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} web = ec.food_web() tops = web.attracting_components() sorted(web.get_label_from_id(n) for c in tops for n in c) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` ['Fox', 'Hawk', 'Marten'] ``` ::: ::: ::: {#09e2e876 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} web.plot( layout="pos", highlight=[n for c in tops for n in c], label_by="label", height=360, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: [Connectivity and flows](../user-guide/connectivity.qmd#directed-graphs) explains why a random walk that enters an attracting component never leaves.
